newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian papers back on streets after month absent.
newsitem.headline: Albanian papers back on streets after month absent.

text.p: Several Albanian daily newspapers resumed publication on Friday after a month-long interruption, in a further sign the country was returning to normal after weeks of unrest.

Two independent titles in Tirana put out their first editions in a month on Friday, raising to four the number of dailies that have returned this week after parliament relaxed restrictions on local media.
Albania and Rilindja ("Renaissance") hit the streets in the capital for the first time since early March.
"For more than a month there was no press coverage," said the independent daily Albania in a front-page editorial on Friday.
"Albania's history will be undocumented for one of its most difficult periods, with more events, pain and doubts for its future," it added.
On Wednesday and Thursday, parliament lifted requirements imposed at the height of the turmoil last month.
The papers had been required to submit articles in advance to government-appointed committees for their approval.
But even despite that move, two major dailies and several smaller titles have still not resumed publication, either for reasons of security or because their offices were damaged in the unrest.
Even newspapers backed by the country's leading political parties were not published during the worst period of violence.
The office of the independent Koha Jone was destroyed in a fire in early March and its publisher was badly beaten in an attack last month in a four-star Tirana hotel.
There are now six daily newspapers in print in Albania: Rilindja Demokratike, Zeri i popullit, Republika, Dita Informacion, Albania and Rilindja.

The previous Albanian government had also temporarily suspended the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) licence to transmit film by satellite from Albania. An emergency all-party government took office on March 14.
Koha Jone and Gazeta Shqiptare are expected to return to print soon.

Western governments and domestic and international watchdog groups had criticised the state of emergency measures for the media as censorship, calling on the government to lift them and for the urgent protection of local journalists.
